None: Um, so let's just go ahead and get started with your background. Maybe tell us a little bit about yourself.

Karthik Narasimhan: Sure, yeah. I'm a professor at Princeton. I've been here for seven years now. I work on broadly research around AI agents just to give a broad term here. But primarily around reinforcement learning and natural language processing, all that. Have been doing that for more than a decade now. I did my PhD back at MIT, and then spent a year at OpenAI. Which was just a really fun time because we actually co-authored the very first GPT paper back then, and it's been crazy to see how that's played out. And yeah, over after that I moved to Princeton. I also spent two years doing a sabbatical at Sierra, which is the new startup that's building agents for the enterprise.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, so let's go ahead and start off, uh, way, way, way back when, um, in undergrad. Um, tell us a little about, about kinda your time at IIT Madras.

Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah. So I was in the computer science program at IIT Madras, and one of the things that I remember about, about the whole college experience was like IIT Madras actually has, like, a pretty comprehensive CS curriculum. We learned not just things in AI but also, like, systems theory, all of that. So it was a, it was a really nice environment just to get, like, a very broad base. And I think one of the things that I really enjoyed was the AI classes obviously, and it was as an undergrad where you're very fascinated with programming and stuff, just thinking about machines automating lots of things is, was just, like, mind-blowing to me, right? And I still vividly remember the sort of, the one class that made me really super interested in AI was this intro to AI class taught by was it Bipa Kimani?

He's like a super senior prof. And we had this very nice, like, project where basically we had to build bots. Multiplayer sort of bots for the game of Snake. And it was, like, a whole competition and everything. So it was, like, a lot of fun just beating out other teams. Think, like 10, almost 15 years ago. Like you're building bots to play against each other and all that. But anyway, it was a lot of, a lot of fun. Made me wanna go deeper into AI and, yeah.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, I guess, like, um, you know, IIT Madras is definitely a pretty hardworking place. Um, and I think you ended up, you know, going to MIT, where you kinda got your master's and PhD. Um, so I guess maybe tell us a little bit about your time at MIT. Um, you know, you were, you started with kind of this broad idea that you wanted to do AI, and, you know, you ended up spending a little bit of time at OpenAI, as we kinda talked about. Um, like, what were so I guess some of, like, kind of the key defining moments during your arc of your PhD?

Karthik Narasimhan: So the PhD is a very, very interesting time I must assure, like I mean folks who didn't even know, right? It's interesting because I think you sort of come in with grand ideas and passion to do things. Then the first one or two years is literally you just, like, reorienting yourself. And trying to figure out, sort of, like, gain a foothold into this whole research community and trying to figure out how do, how do you even do research? How do you write papers, all that, right? So I, yeah, I went to MIT and my to be under Regina Barzilay's lab. She's like a pioneer in NLP, and more specifically actually, like language grounding. You know one of her prior students former students, like, Bronovan, he'd written, like, a really classic paper on, like, how you can use you know NLP to improve RL agents. Like, it's still, it's still to this day I consider one of the defining papers.

It sort of went under the radar, I feel, but, like, it basically taught a bot how to read the manual and play Civilization, which is, like, the coolest thing ever, which was the coolest thing I ever heard at that point for me. And yeah I went there. One of the things that I really had to learn from scratch was just, like just being proactive. Figuring out things on your own, being independent. I think I had all these qualities before, but, like, I cannot emphasize how important that is, right when you're a PhD student and you sort of want to make progress or, like, figure out your niche, right? So I think those, those things are probably far more important than your IQ level or, you know how how you, how you actually, like, how smart you are and things like that.

So anyway, so I think that was the PhD was a really rewarding experience. Started off working on some core NLP tasks. Things like information extraction and some kind of, like sentiment analysis, all that. But then very quickly I figured out my love for RL was still there, and this was actually because of I would credit my undergrad prof here, like, Ravindra, Professor Ravindra, and he's still at IIT Madras. Like, he taught this RL course which was, like, so interesting, so fascinating. So I kept thinking about RL, right? And So, yeah, the last I would say, like, from the third year onwards, like, most of my PhD was you know, devoted to this language grounding area, where you're basically using reinforcement learning to teach these systems how to understand language. Right. Just like how you're doing or I'm doing as humans.

But yeah, overall it was great. Like I feel like the PhD gives you the time and space to really go deep on something that unfortunately you don't get after in a graduate program.

None: Yeah. Awesome. Um, and, and I think kind of broadly there's a few different areas that you've worked on, like, one is RL. Um, you had, like, HDQN back in 2016.

Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah.

None: Uh, you had a paper on multi-objective RL back in 2019. Um, and then I think kind of early on you also had a paper on, like, Text DQN, which was actually back in 2015. And then over time, um, you know, we, we talked about, you know, kind of how you had worked on GPT, um, at OpenAI. Um, so maybe we can touch upon that. But then also kind of over time it seems like you kind of switched over to, like, you know, language agents with, like, Koala in 2023, SWE-Agent in 2024, and then a little bit of kind of some work in, like, maybe datasets and benchmarks. Like, obviously SWE-Bench, um, which, you know, we had John Yang on the podcast as well, you know, TAO-Bench, um, things like this. So maybe tell us a little about kind of why you switched over from, like, the RL world maybe, um, and maybe a little bit of language models to kind of this more benchmarks and language agents world, um, kind of the motivation of that arc. And then maybe tell us a little about your time after your PhD and, um, kind of your arc since then.

Karthik Narasimhan: I would consider myself an NLP person, go to NLP conferences and like, from the outside I'm, I was an NLP researcher, but inside really I just like, like I said, right? One of the, one of the first classes I took it was more about broadly about AI, right? And if I look back in hindsight, it's like even if you consider this whole grounding aspect to it. It's basically the feeling that I always had, like, language doesn't exist in isolation. So you shouldn't solve language in isolation, right? So I would say it's not really like a specific, like, pre-defined arc or something. Like, go from RL to this and this. The one guiding sort of principle I always try to, try to strive for is to try and basically push the envelope and define new areas.

And you know, there's sort of, like, several different kinds of research you can do, right? You can develop new models that solve really challenging tasks. You can sort of be really good at, like, empirical analysis and, like, have, like, really nice papers that showcase the different strengths and weaknesses. But I feel like the place that I'm most comfortable is, like, just trying to imagine one or two steps into the future and try to bring that and close the gap between what we're seeing now and that. So I think most of the things that you just talked about have that flavor. I wouldn't say I'm, like specifically oriented towards methods or benchmarking. I think all of these are necessary. And they're necessary. It's kind of like a cycle, right? Like, I mean, at some point you feel like you do wanna see new tasks that you want these systems to be performing, not just answering questions, right?

And so that sort of, like, prompts you to be like, "Okay, what is useful in this real world-" kind of scenario. And all that. So I think SWE-Bench, TAO-Bench, those are sort of like even WebShop, I would say, like, those are sort of, like, pushing, trying to push towards, like, "Hey, let's not just get these systems to play Atari games." Which is cool. Which is great. But I think they are more capable than that, so let's go let's move past that.

astra.text:
Yeah, I think for me, like, a big part of the appeal was the freedom to define your own research agenda, right? To sort of say, “Okay, here's something that I think is going to be interesting in five years. Let's spend some time figuring it out.” And you get to build a group of people who are excited about those questions and bring their own perspectives to them. That was really appealing to me.

And then the other piece is working with students. I mean, I talked about how much my professors influenced me, both in undergrad and during my PhD. I think there's something really rewarding about being on the other side of that, right? You get to see someone come in, start figuring out how to do research, and then eventually they're coming up with ideas that you wouldn't have thought of yourself. That's a really exciting process.

So, yeah, OpenAI was a great environment, and I really enjoyed the people there. But having the opportunity to build a lab, work with students, and explore this broader set of questions around language and learning and agents—that was something I really wanted to try.

sol.text:
Yeah, I mean, it was definitely a hard choice because OpenAI was such an exciting place. But I think what really drew me to academia was the freedom to define my own research agenda and pursue questions that might take several years to play out. Like I said, the kind of research I enjoy most is imagining one or two steps into the future and trying to close that gap, and a university is a really nice environment for doing that.

The other big part was working with students. I had benefited so much from mentors at IIT Madras and MIT, and I really liked the idea of building a group, helping students develop their own taste in problems, and watching them become independent researchers. So it wasn't really that I wanted to leave OpenAI; it was more that Princeton offered this combination of intellectual freedom, long-term thinking, and mentorship that felt like the right fit for me.

opus.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly the answer is a little less dramatic than people expect, because the Princeton thing was sort of already in motion, right? Like, I'd gone through the faculty job market during my PhD, and I had accepted the offer, and then the OpenAI thing came up and it was basically a "come do this for a year before you start" kind of arrangement. So it wasn't like I was sitting there at OpenAI agonizing, like, "Do I stay or do I go?" The decision had kind of already been made, and the year was almost like a bonus round.

But, I mean, why academia in the first place? I think two things. One is students. And I say this now having done it for seven years, like, it's genuinely the best part of the job. You get to work with these incredibly smart people who are at the point in their lives where they're figuring out what they care about, and you get to be a part of that. That, that's just not something you get anywhere else. Even at a place as good as OpenAI was, you're hiring people who already know what they're doing.

And the second thing is, is just the freedom, right? Like, a lab, even a research lab, and even back then when it was a nonprofit, there's, there's this gravitational pull towards whatever the big bet is. And that's, I mean that's correct, that's how you get the big thing done, right? But it means the set of things you can work on kind of narrows over time. Whereas in academia you can be, you can be deliberately orthogonal. You can say, "Everybody's scaling, so let me go think about what happens after scaling works." And I think a lot of the stuff we ended up doing, like WebShop, SWE-Bench, that, that only happens if you have the room to chase something that isn't obviously the main thing yet.

The tradeoff is compute, obviously. (laughs) Like, I'm not gonna pretend there isn't compute envy. But I've never really regretted it.

Yeah, I mean it was super tempting, right? OpenAI was just this, like, incredibly fun place — well-funded research lab, nonprofit at the time, people who were super warm and super smart, and you could go from low-level details to AGI in the same conversation. So it wasn’t that I didn’t like it. I loved it.

But I think the thing that really pulled me toward academia was the same thing I had to learn during the PhD, which is independence. Like, being proactive, figuring out your own niche, having the time and space to go deep on something. I always felt language doesn’t exist in isolation, and the work I wanted to do was a little more… imagining one or two steps into the future and then trying to close that gap. Defining new areas, not just iterating on whatever the hottest model or game is right now.

And industry is amazing for that in some ways — you have compute, you have product pressure, you see real users — but I felt like a faculty job gave me more of that longer horizon. You can work on things that aren’t obviously useful yet. You can bounce between methods and benchmarks and agents, whatever the problem needs. I wouldn’t say I’m specifically a methods person or a benchmarking person; it’s more of a cycle. And Princeton felt like a place where I could actually do that with students, over years, not just over a product cycle.

I still like the industry side a lot — I mean I later spent two years on sabbatical at Sierra building agents for the enterprise — so it wasn’t like I was running away from that world. It was more that I wanted a home base where I could keep pushing on the research questions I cared about, with that kind of freedom. And yeah, seven years later, I still think that was the right call.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so part of it was that I actually already had the offer from Princeton and had accepted it before going to OpenAI. Princeton was gracious enough to let me defer my start date for a year, which allowed me to spend that time at OpenAI. 

But fundamentally, I think it came down to two main things. First is working with students. I just really love mentoring and teaching. There's something deeply rewarding about having a student join your lab, helping them navigate those first couple of uncertain years, and then watching them grow into completely independent, world-class researchers who are driving their own agendas. That’s an experience you just don't get anywhere else.

And the second thing is intellectual freedom. Even back then, while OpenAI was a fantastic place to do research, you could sort of see things starting to coalesce around specific, large-scale bets. Which was clearly the right move for them, given how things turned out! But in academia, you have the freedom to pursue whatever crazy, curiosity-driven ideas you want. You can jump across different subfields, define new benchmarks, explore weird intersections between RL and language, and you don't have to align with an organizational roadmap or worry about near-term utility. 

So I always felt that pull towards having my own lab, setting my own agenda, and working with students. And Princeton has just been an amazing place to do that.

kimi.text:
Yeah, I think for me, I feel like I always knew, like, deep down, that I wanted to be an academic. Even when I was going to grad school, I think the professor route was sort of, like, the default thing I had in mind. And I think a big part of it is just the freedom, right? Like, the PhD really taught me the value of having the time and space to go deep on a problem that you're curious about, without having to justify it against, like, a product roadmap or, like, quarterly milestones or anything like that. And I think in academia you're able to sort of set your own agenda, pick problems that you think are one or two steps into the future, and just kind of go at them, even if nobody else believes in them yet. Which, like, back then, remember, it wasn't at all obvious that industry labs were going to become, like, the center of gravity for this kind of research. So it was a very different calculation from what people face today.

The other part honestly is the students. Like, I really enjoy working with students, mentoring them, watching them go from, like, not knowing how research works to becoming these totally independent researchers. That's incredibly rewarding, and you just don't get that in the same way in industry. And Princeton specifically was just, like, a fantastic place. Great colleagues, amazing students, and a lot of flexibility to pursue the things I wanted. So yeah, I had a great time at OpenAI, and I sort of consider, like, did I want to stay longer, but I think I never really doubted that academia was where I wanted to end up. And it's worked out pretty well, so no regrets.

fable.text:
Yeah, so I get asked this a lot, actually. And honestly, I mean, the PhD, like I said, right, it sort of gave me this taste of being able to go deep on something for, like, a long time and, and really own a direction. And I think when I was at OpenAI, it was amazing, but you're also sort of part of this bigger machine, right? Like, there's this cauldron of ideas, but at the end of the day there's a certain set of bets the org is making, and you're sort of, like, plugging into one of those. And I think for me, the thing that I kept coming back to was, like, what I'm most excited about is trying to imagine what's one or two steps ahead and then go define that area, right? And academia is just, like, uniquely set up for that. Nobody's telling you what to work on. You can go work on some weird thing, like, teaching agents to shop on the web or whatever, and if it doesn't pan out for two years, that's, that's fine, right? Like, that's the job.

And the other big thing, honestly, was students. Like, I had really, really great advisors and mentors, and I think there's something really rewarding about, like, taking someone who's coming in with all this passion and, like, helping them figure out how to do research. And also, like, they teach you a lot, right? Like, students come in with, like, totally fresh perspectives, they're not constrained by, like, "Oh, this is how things have always been done." So a lot of the things you mentioned, like SWE-Bench, TAO-Bench, those are, like, really students driving that.

And then, I mean, I'll be honest, it's also just, like, timing, right? This was 2018. OpenAI was not what it is today. It was, like, a nonprofit research lab, it wasn't obvious what the trajectory was gonna be. So it didn't feel like I was leaving, like, this rocket ship or something. And, and I think the nice thing about being an academic is you can still go back and forth, right? Like, I did a sabbatical at Sierra, I still collaborate with folks in industry. So it's not like a one-way door. Yeah.
